2 Geometric framework

In this section, we provide the geometric set-up and the definition of various quantities that will be use throughout the paper. We also present the equations and the coordinates that will be used in the proofs.

2.1 Spherically symmetric initial data set

To obtain a spherically symmetric space-time, we work with spherically symmetric initial data and this symmetry is then transmitted to the solution (c.f. [28]). Such a strategy is standard, so we only briefly recall some key definitions.

Definition 2.1.

An initial data set of the Cauchy problem for (1.1), (1.2), (1.3), (1.4), (1.5) is given by a septuplet (Σ(3),hi​j,Ki​j,ϕ0,ϕ0′,Ei,Bi)(\Sigma^{(3)},h_{ij},K_{ij},\phi_{0},\phi^{\prime}_{0},E_{i},B_{i}), where (Σ(3),hi​j)(\Sigma^{(3)},h_{ij}) is a three-dimensional Riemannian manifold, Ki​jK_{ij} is a symmetric tensor, ϕ0\phi_{0}, ϕ0′\phi^{\prime}_{0} are complex-valued scalar functions on Σ(3)\Sigma^{(3)}, and EiE_{i} (the electric field), BiB_{i} (the magnetic field) are vectors on Σ(3)\Sigma^{(3)}.

Remark 2.1.

The Cauchy problem for (1.1), (1.2), (1.3), (1.4), (1.5) is locally well-posed, see [28], [6]: for regular data (Σ(3),…)(\Sigma^{(3)},...) satisfying the constraints, there exists a solution (M,g,ϕ,F)(M,g,\phi,F) and a coordinate system (t,x1,x2,x3)(t,x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}) such that

Σ(3)={t=0},\Sigma^{(3)}=\{t=0\},
hi​j=g|Σ(3),h_{ij}=g_{|\Sigma^{(3)}},
Ki​j=ℒ∂tg|Σ(3),K_{ij}=\mathcal{L}_{\partial_{t}}g_{|\Sigma^{(3)}},
ϕ0=ϕ|Σ(3),\phi_{0}=\phi_{|\Sigma^{(3)}},
ϕ′0=Dtϕ|Σ(3),\phi^{\prime}_{0}=D_{t}\phi_{|\Sigma^{(3)}},
Ei=F(∂t,∂i),E_{i}=F(\partial_{t},\partial_{i}),
Bi=∗F(∂t,∂i).B_{i}=*F(\partial_{t},\partial_{i}).

In fact, there exists a unique globally hyperbolic solution (M,g,ϕ,F)(M,g,\phi,F) which is also maximal (c.f. [6] for precise definitions). We call (M,g,ϕ,F)(M,g,\phi,F) the maximal (globally hyperbolic) development of the initial data (Σ(3),hi​j,Ki​j,ϕ0,ϕ0′,Ei,Bi)(\Sigma^{(3)},h_{ij},K_{ij},\phi_{0},\phi^{\prime}_{0},E_{i},B_{i}).

Definition 2.2 ([28]).

We say that (M,g,ϕ,F)(M,g,\phi,F), the maximal development of (Σ(3),…)(\Sigma^{(3)},...), is spherically symmetric if

  1. 1.

    The Lie group S​O​(3)SO(3) acts smoothly by isometry on (Σ(3),hi​j)(\Sigma^{(3)},h_{ij}).

  2. 2.

    The action of S​O​(3)SO(3) leaves KK, ϕ0\phi_{0}, ϕ0′\phi^{\prime}_{0}, EE and BB invariant.

  3. 3.

    Σ(3)/S​O​(3)\Sigma^{(3)}/SO(3) can be equipped with the structure of a one-dimensional Riemmanian manifold-with-boundary.

As a result, we obtain a smooth S​O​(3)SO(3) action on (M,g)(M,g) by isometry, with spacelike orbits. Then, one defines the quotient M/S​O​(3)M/SO(3) which we conformally embed into a bounded subset of (ℝ1+1,mμ,ν)(\mathbb{R}^{1+1},m_{\mu,\nu}). We denote the embedding as 𝒬\mathcal{Q} (a bounded subset of ℝ1+1\mathbb{R}^{1+1}). We also denote 𝒬+\mathcal{Q}^{+}, the future domain of dependence in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of the conformal image of Σ(3)/S​O​(3)\Sigma^{(3)}/SO(3) in ℝ1+1\mathbb{R}^{1+1}. We also define ℬ+\mathcal{B}^{+} as the boundary of 𝒬+\mathcal{Q}^{+} induced by the ambient ℝ1+1\mathbb{R}^{1+1} (i.e. the limit points of 𝒬+\mathcal{Q}^{+} as a subset of ℝ1+1\mathbb{R}^{1+1}) and subsequently the bounded domain-with-boundary 𝒬+¯:=𝒬+∪ℬ+⊂ℝ1+1\overline{\mathcal{Q}^{+}}:=\mathcal{Q}^{+}\cup\mathcal{B}^{+}\subset\mathbb{R}^{1+1} (see Proposition 2.1 and its discussion in [28] for details).

Definition 2.3.

We call Π:M→𝒬\Pi:M\rightarrow\mathcal{Q} the natural projection taking a point to its group orbit. Note that for all p∈𝒬p\in\mathcal{Q}, Π−1​(p)\Pi^{-1}(p) is isometric to a sphere. We then define the area-radius function rr on 𝒬\mathcal{Q} by the formula

r⁡(p)=A​r​e​a​(Π−1​(p))4​π.r(p)=\sqrt{\frac{Area(\Pi^{-1}(p))}{4\pi}}.

The metric gg on MM is then given by

g=g𝒬+r2​d​σ𝕊2,g=g_{\mathcal{Q}}+r^{2}d\sigma_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}, (2.1)

where d​σ𝕊2d\sigma_{\mathbb{S}^{2}} is the standard metric on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} and g𝒬g_{\mathcal{Q}} is a Lorentzian metric on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

We will denote Γ⊂𝒬\Gamma\subset\mathcal{Q}, that we call the center of symmetry, the set of fixed points under the S​O​(3)SO(3) action on MM (which we identify with its image under Π\Pi). Notice that, by definition, r|Γ=0r_{|\Gamma}=0.

2.2 Metric in double null coordinates

g𝒬g_{\mathcal{Q}} defined in (2.1) is a 1+11+1 Lorentzian metric and, as such, is conformally flat: thus, there exists coordinates (u,v)(u,v), which we call null coordinates, on (𝒬,g𝒬)(\mathcal{Q},g_{\mathcal{Q}}) and a function Ω2​(u,v)\Omega^{2}(u,v) such that

g𝒬:=−Ω2​(u,v)2​(d​u⊗d​v+d​v⊗d​u)g_{\mathcal{Q}}:=-\frac{\Omega^{2}(u,v)}{2}(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du)

In view of this formalism, we consider (abusing notation) the area-radius rr as a function r⁡(u,v)r(u,v) on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. In fact, one can use the coordinate system (u,v,θ,φ)(u,v,\theta,\varphi) on MM where (θ,φ)(\theta,\varphi) are the standard coordinates on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}. Thus, (2.1) becomes

g=−Ω2​(u,v)2(du⊗dv+dv⊗du)+r2(u,v)(dθ2+sin(θ)2dφ2).g=-\frac{\Omega^{2}(u,v)}{2}(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du)+r^{2}(u,v)(d\theta^{2}+\sin(\theta)^{2}d\varphi^{2}).
Remark 2.2.

The choice of null coordinates is not unique: one can renormalize (u,v)(u,v) into new null coordinates (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) by the identities d​u~=f⁡(u)​d​ud\tilde{u}=f(u)du, d​v~=g⁡(v)​d​vd\tilde{v}=g(v)dv for any strictly positive function ff and gg. Notice that, upon this change of coordinate, Ω2\Omega^{2} is also changed by the formula Ω~2​d​u~​d​v~=Ω2​d​u​d​v\tilde{\Omega}^{2}d\tilde{u}d\tilde{v}=\Omega^{2}dudv i.e. Ω~2​(u,v)=f​(u)−1⋅g​(v)−1⋅Ω2​(u,v)\tilde{\Omega}^{2}(u,v)=f(u)^{-1}\cdot g(v)^{-1}\cdot\Omega^{2}(u,v).

Remark 2.3.

To draw a Penrose diagram (see Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), we choose (u,v)(u,v) to be in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, a bounded subset of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and we draw 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Since 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} are conformally isometric, it is a standard fact that they have the same causal structure.

Now, we will use this coordinate system (u,v)(u,v) to define important quantities. We abuse notation denote FF the push-forward by Π\Pi of the original 2-form over MM, and the same for ϕ\phi. The spherically symmetric character (c.f. [28]) of FF imposes that there exists a scalar function Q⁡(u,v)Q(u,v) (independent of the coordinate choice), called the charge, such that

F=Q2​r2​Ω2​d​u∧d​v.F=\frac{Q}{2r^{2}}\Omega^{2}du\wedge dv.
Remark 2.4.

In our setting, the scalar field is charged, hence (1.4) is an inhomogeneous Maxwell equation, and Q⁡(u,v)Q(u,v) is a scalar function. This is in contrast with the uncharged case where Q≡e∈ℝQ\equiv e\in\mathbb{R}, c.f. remarks 1.11 and 1.14.

Subsequently, we define the Lorentzian gradient of rr, and introduce the mass ratio μ\mu by the formula

1−μ:=g𝒬​(∇r,∇r)=−4∂ur⋅∂vrΩ2.1-\mu:=g_{\mathcal{Q}}(\nabla r,\nabla r)=\frac{-4\partial_{u}r\cdot\partial_{v}r}{\Omega^{2}}.

μ\mu is independent of the coordinate choice. We define the Hawking mass ρ\rho (also independent of the coordinates choice):

ρ:=μ⋅r2=r2⋅(1−g𝒬​(∇r,∇r)),\rho:=\frac{\mu\cdot r}{2}=\frac{r}{2}\cdot(1-g_{\mathcal{Q}}(\nabla r,\nabla r)),

and the modified mass ϖ\varpi, the last quantity which is independent of the coordinates choice, also involving the charge QQ:

ϖ:=ρ+Q22​r=μ​r2+Q22​r.\varpi:=\rho+\frac{Q^{2}}{2r}=\frac{\mu r}{2}+\frac{Q^{2}}{2r}. (2.2)

Now, we introduce notations for coordinate-dependent quantities: the ingoing derivative of rr in (u,v)(u,v) coordinates:

ν⁡(u,v):=∂ur⁡(u,v),\nu(u,v):=\partial_{u}r(u,v), (2.3)

followed by the outgoing derivative of rr in (u,v)(u,v) coordinates :

λ⁡(u,v):=∂vr⁡(u,v).\lambda(u,v):=\partial_{v}r(u,v). (2.4)

Then, we define κ∈ℝ∪{±∞}\kappa\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\} by the following formula, also using the previous notations:

κ=λ1−2​ρr=−Ω24​ν,\kappa=\frac{\lambda}{1-\frac{2\rho}{r}}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}=\frac{-\Omega^{2}}{4\nu}, (2.5)

and its “outgoing” analogue ι∈ℝ∪{±∞}\iota\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}

ι=ν1−2​ρr=−Ω24​λ.\iota=\frac{\nu}{1-\frac{2\rho}{r}}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}=\frac{-\Omega^{2}}{4\lambda}. (2.6)

We summarize all the relations between the different quantities:

1−μ=1−2​ρr=1−2​ϖr+Q2r2=−4​ν​λΩ2=κ−1⋅λ=ι−1⋅ν.1-\mu=1-\frac{2\rho}{r}=1-\frac{2\varpi}{r}+\frac{Q^{2}}{r^{2}}=\frac{-4\nu\lambda}{\Omega^{2}}=\kappa^{-1}\cdot\lambda=\iota^{-1}\cdot\nu. (2.7)

2.3 The Reissner–Nordström solution

The sub-extremal Reissner–Nordström space-time of mass M>0M>0 and charge e∈(0,M)e\in(0,M) is a two-ended (see section 2.7) spherically symmetric black hole solving the system (1.1), (1.2), (1.3), (1.4), (1.5) for ϕ≡0\phi\equiv 0, whose metric is given by

gR​N=−(1−2​Mr+e2r2)−1dt2+(1−2​Mr+e2r2)dr2+r2(dθ2+sin(θ)2dφ2),g_{RN}=-(1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}})^{-1}dt^{2}+(1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}})dr^{2}+r^{2}(d\theta^{2}+\sin(\theta)^{2}d\varphi^{2}),

and in the coordinate system (t,r,θ,φ)(t,r,\theta,\varphi), ∂t\partial_{t} is a time-like Killing vector field. We define null coordinates u=r∗−t2u=\frac{r^{*}-t}{2}, v=r∗+t2v=\frac{r^{*}+t}{2}, where r∗r^{*} is defined by the d​r∗d​r=−(1−2​Mr+e2r2)−1\frac{dr^{*}}{dr}=-(1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}})^{-1}. Thus, the metric can be re-written in (u,v,θ,φ)(u,v,\theta_{,}\varphi) coordinates as

gR​N=−2(1−2​Mr+e2r2)(du⊗dv+dv⊗du)+r2(u,v)(dθ2+sin(θ)2dφ2).g_{RN}=-2(1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}})(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du)+r^{2}(u,v)(d\theta^{2}+\sin(\theta)^{2}d\varphi^{2}).

The polynomial r2−2​M​r+e2=r2​(1−2​Mr+e2r2)r^{2}-2Mr+e^{2}=r^{2}(1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}}) admits two distinct roots r±​(M,e)=M±M2−e2r_{\pm}(M,e)=M\pm\sqrt{M^{2}-e^{2}}, as e∈(0,M)e\in(0,M). Note that r∗​(r±)=∓∞r^{*}(r_{\pm})=\mp\infty. Even after we fix a double null coordinate system (u,v)(u,v), an electromagnetic gauge freedom subsist.

|ϕ|​(u2,v)≤|ϕ|​(u1,v)+∫u1u2|Du​ϕ|​(u′,v)​d​u′,|\phi|(u_{2},v)\leq|\phi|(u_{1},v)+\int_{u_{1}}^{u_{2}}|D_{u}\phi|(u^{\prime},v)du^{\prime},

for some u0∈ℝu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}. Although the gauge choice is irrelevant for gauge invariant estimates, Dv​ϕ=∂vϕD_{v}\phi=\partial_{v}\phi in practice by (2.21).

2.6 Trapped region and apparent horizon

We define the trapped region 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the regular region ℛ\mathcal{R} and the apparent horizon 𝒜\mathcal{A} using (2.7), as

  1. 1.

    (u,v)∈𝒯(u,v)\in\mathcal{T} if and only if 1−2​ρ​(u,v)r⁡(u,v)<01-\frac{2\rho(u,v)}{r(u,v)}<0 if and only if λ⁡(u,v)<0\lambda(u,v)<0 and ν⁡(u,v)<0\nu(u,v)<0,

  2. 2.

    (u,v)∈ℛ(u,v)\in\mathcal{R} if and only if 1−2​ρ​(u,v)r⁡(u,v)>01-\frac{2\rho(u,v)}{r(u,v)}>0 if and only if either λ⁡(u,v)>0\lambda(u,v)>0 and ν⁡(u,v)<0\nu(u,v)<0 or λ⁡(u,v)<0\lambda(u,v)<0 and ν⁡(u,v)>0\nu(u,v)>0.

  3. 3.

    (u,v)∈𝒜(u,v)\in\mathcal{A} if and only if 1−2​ρ​(u,v)r⁡(u,v)=01-\frac{2\rho(u,v)}{r(u,v)}=0 if and only if λ⁡(u,v)⋅ν⁡(u,v)=0\lambda(u,v)\cdot\nu(u,v)=0.

Note that, for admissible space-times (in the sense of Definition 2.6), the case λ⁡(u,v)>0\lambda(u,v)>0 and ν⁡(u,v)>0\nu(u,v)>0 i.e. that (u,v)(u,v) is an anti-trapped surface never occurs.

Notice also, that, for one-ended admissible space-times, ν<0\nu<0 everywhere so the occurrence of a trapped surface in (u,v)(u,v) depends only on the sign of λ⁡(u,v)\lambda(u,v). Moreover, for two ended admissible space-times, there exists a neighborhood of 𝒞​ℋi1+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}_{1}} on which ν<0\nu<0. Therefore, the following characterisation is pertinent: over 𝒟:={(u,v)/ν(u,v)<0}\mathcal{D}:=\{(u,v)/\nu(u,v)<0\}, we have:

  1. 1.

    (u,v)∈𝒯(u,v)\in\mathcal{T} if and only if λ⁡(u,v)<0\lambda(u,v)<0.

  2. 2.

    (u,v)∈ℛ(u,v)\in\mathcal{R} if and only if λ⁡(u,v)>0\lambda(u,v)>0.

  3. 3.

    (u,v)∈𝒜(u,v)\in\mathcal{A} if and only if if and only if λ⁡(u,v)=0\lambda(u,v)=0.

It is in fact this final characterization that we will use.

Note also that for one-ended admissible space-time, as r|Γ=0r_{|\Gamma}=0, we have Γ⊂ℛ\Gamma\subset\mathcal{R}.

2.7 Topology of the initial data: the one-ended case and the two-ended case

In this section, we define mathematically the notion of one-ended or two-ended space-times, following [28].

Definition 2.4.

We say that (M,gμ​ν,ϕ,Fμ​ν)(M,g_{\mu\nu},\phi,F_{\mu\nu}) is the maximal development of spherically symmetric one-ended initial data if (M,gμ​ν,ϕ,Fμ​ν)(M,g_{\mu\nu},\phi,F_{\mu\nu}) is the future maximal globally hyperbolic development of (Σ(3),hi​j,Ki​j,ϕ0,ϕ0′,Q0)(\Sigma^{(3)},h_{ij},K_{ij},\phi_{0},\phi^{\prime}_{0},Q_{0}) and Σ(3)\Sigma^{(3)} is diffeomorphic to ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}.

Definition 2.5.

We say that (M,gμ​ν,ϕ,Fμ​ν)(M,g_{\mu\nu},\phi,F_{\mu\nu}) is the maximal development of spherically symmetric two-ended initial data if (M,gμ​ν,ϕ,Fμ​ν)(M,g_{\mu\nu},\phi,F_{\mu\nu}) is the future maximal globally hyperbolic development of (Σ(3),hi​j,Ki​j,ϕ0,ϕ0′,Q0)(\Sigma^{(3)},h_{ij},K_{ij},\phi_{0},\phi^{\prime}_{0},Q_{0}) and Σ(3)\Sigma^{(3)} is diffeomorphic to 𝕊2×ℝ\mathbb{S}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}.

Remark 2.5.

The results of Theorem 0.1 and Theorem 0.2 prove that in the two-ended case Γ=∅\Gamma=\emptyset, while in the one-ended case Γ\Gamma is connected, time-like, and non-empty.

Definition 2.6.

We say that (Σ(3),hi​j,Ki​j,ϕ0,ϕ0′,Q0)(\Sigma^{(3)},h_{ij},K_{ij},\phi_{0},\phi^{\prime}_{0},Q_{0}) is an admissible data set

  1. 1.

    in the one-ended case, if there exists no anti-trapped surface on Σ(3)\Sigma^{(3)} in the sense that ν|Σ0<0\nu_{|\Sigma_{0}}<0.

  2. 2.

    in the two-ended case, if there exists u1<u2u_{1}<u_{2} such that ν|Σ0(u)<0\nu_{|\Sigma_{0}}(u)<0 for all u≤u2u\leq u_{2} and λ|Σ0(u)<0\lambda_{|\Sigma_{0}}(u)<0 for all u≥u1u\geq u_{1}.

Remark 2.6.

Note that the particularity of two-ended admissible data sets is that they already contain a trapped surface, hence their maximal development feature a black hole. Thus the two-ended case does not allow for trapped surfaces (hence black holes) to form dynamically, in contrast with the one-ended case, suitable to study gravitational collapse.

2.8 Notions of inextendibility

In this section, we define two notions of C2C^{2}-inextendibility: the first one is standard and can be found in [32]. The second one is the C2C^{2}-inextendibility across 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}, a new (but analogous) notion which we use in the one-ended case, as there exists an additional obstruction to C2C^{2}-inextendibility in this case, related to Weak Cosmic Censorship (see section 1.5).

Definition 2.7.

We consider (M,gμ​ν,ϕ,Fμ​ν)(M,g_{\mu\nu},\phi,F_{\mu\nu}) the maximal development of smooth, spherically symmetric and admissible (in the sense of Definition 2.6) one-ended or two-ended initial data satisfying the Einstein–Maxwell–Klein–Gordon system.   1. 1.

    For every p∈M~−i⁡(M)p\in\tilde{M}-i(M), I+​(p)∩i⁡(M)=∅I^{+}(p)\cap i(M)=\emptyset.

If no such extension exists, we say that (M,g)(M,g) is C2C^{2}-future-inextendible.

Definition 2.8.

We consider (M,gμ​ν,ϕ,F)(M,g_{\mu\nu},\phi,F) the maximal development of smooth, spherically symmetric and admissible (in the sense of Definition 2.6) one-ended initial data satisfying the Einstein–Maxwell–Klein–Gordon system. ℬ+=bΓ∪𝒮Γ1∪𝒮Γ2∪𝒮∪𝒮i+∪𝒞​ℋi+∪i+∪ℐ+∪i0.\mathcal{B_{+}}=b_{\Gamma}\cup\mathcal{S}_{\Gamma}^{1}\cup\mathcal{S}_{\Gamma}^{2}\cup\mathcal{S}\cup\mathcal{S}_{i^{+}}\cup\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}\cup i^{+}\cup\mathcal{I}^{+}\cup i^{0}.

Then we say that (M¯,g)(\overline{M},g) is C2C^{2}-future-extendible across 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} if there exists a differentiable manifold M~\tilde{M} equipped with a C2C^{2} Lorentzian metric g~\tilde{g} and a smooth isometric embedding i:M→M~i:M\rightarrow\tilde{M}, such that i⁡(M)i(M) is a proper subset of M~\tilde{M} and moreover the following conditions hold true:

    There exists p∈∂Mp\in\partial M, where ∂M\partial M is the topological boundary of i⁡(M)i(M) in M~\tilde{M}, at which ∂M\partial M is differentiable and a continuous curve γ:(−ϵ,ϵ)→M~\gamma:(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\rightarrow\tilde{M} with γ⁡(0)=p\gamma(0)=p, γ⁡(−ϵ,0)⊂M\gamma(-\epsilon,0)\subset M and moreover Π⁡(γ⁡(−ϵ,0))¯𝒬+∩𝒞​ℋi+≠∅.\overline{\Pi(\gamma(-\epsilon,0))}^{\mathcal{Q}^{+}}\cap\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}\neq\emptyset.

In practice, we always identify MM with i⁡(M)i(M) to lighten the notation when possible, as these two manifolds are isometric.

3 Precise statement of the main results

In this section, we describe the results of section 1.2 in a more precise way. We will work with the conventions, notations and definitions of Theorem 0.1, Theorem 0.2 and section 2. When there is no risk of confusion, we will use the notation 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} to denote any Cauchy horizon emanating from time-like infinity, in both the one-ended or the two-ended case.

In this section, we rephrase the results of [47] in a way which is convenient to use in our setting. The assumptions of the following theorem are also the basic assumptions we will rely on during the entire paper.

The result of [47] is local in a neighborhood of i+i^{+} and thus, can be applied indifferently to the one-ended or two-ended case. For convenience, we rephrase the statement of the theorem of [47] into a one-ended case, and a two-ended case.

Remark 3.1.

We emphasize that the statement of Theorem 3.1 was originally formulated in [47] as a characteristic initial value problem, with data on ℋ+∪𝒞i​n\mathcal{H}^{+}\cup\mathcal{C}_{in} thus the global topology of the Penrose diagram was irrelevant and the statement was identical in both the one-ended and the two-ended case. However, in the present paper, the distinction between one and two ended is somewhat important, which is why we phrased the theorem in this way.

Remark 3.2.

Note that assumption 3 consists of four statements

  1. i

    ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} is an event horizon i.e.

    lim supv→+∞r|ℋ+(v)<+∞.\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}r_{|\mathcal{H}^{+}}(v)<+\infty.
  2. ii

    ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} possesses a finite asymptotic charge i.e.

    lim supv→+∞|Q||ℋ+(v)<+∞.\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|Q|_{|\mathcal{H}^{+}}(v)<+\infty.
  3. iii

    ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} is asymptotically a Reissner–Nordström event horizon i.e. the asymptotic charge is non-zero i.e.

    lim supv→+∞|Q||ℋ+(v)>0.\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|Q|_{|\mathcal{H}^{+}}(v)>0.
  4. iv

    ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} is asymptotically a sub-extremal (Reissner–Nordström) event horizon

    lim supv→+∞|Q||ℋ+(v)≠lim supv→+∞r|ℋ+(v).\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|Q|_{|\mathcal{H}^{+}}(v)\neq\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}r_{|\mathcal{H}^{+}}(v).

Note that the sub-assumption ii is in fact unnecessary (although we add it for clarity), as it follows from sub-assumption i and the decay of the initial data dictated by assumption 4, c.f. [47].

Assumption iii is important: indeed, if the asymptotic charge is zero instead i.e. ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} is asymptotically a Schwarzschild event horizon, then the author proved that no Cauchy horizon is present: 𝒞​ℋi+=∅\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}=\emptyset, thus r=0r=0 on ℬ+\mathcal{B}^{+}, see [49], section 2.3.4. Note, however, that the asymptotic charge is conjectured to be non-zero generically, see [28].

Notice that sub-assumption iv requiring ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} to be a sub-extremal is superfluous in the uncharged case q0=0q_{0}=0 where the event horizon is necessarily sub-extremal (see Appendix A of [32]), a property which does not persist in the charged q0≠0q_{0}\neq 0. The sub-extremality of the event horizon is also conjectured to be generic, c.f. [28].

We are now ready to phrase our new global results, starting from the C2C^{2}-inextendibility of the Cauchy horizon.

3.2 Global inextendibility properties across the Cauchy horizon emanating from i+i^{+}

In this section, we present our C2C^{2}-inextendibility (defined in section 2.8) results, starting with the two-ended case:

Theorem 3.2.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be the maximal development of admissible two-ended initial data, satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 3.1. Then (M,g)(M,g) is C2C^{2}-future-inextendible.

In the one-ended case, additional complications arise because of the potential existence of an “outgoing Cauchy horizon” emanating from the center 𝒞​ℋΓ\mathcal{CH}_{\Gamma}. Since this 𝒞​ℋΓ\mathcal{CH}_{\Gamma} could be C2C^{2}-extendible, we only prove the C2C^{2}-inextendibility of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}:

Theorem 3.3.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be the maximal development of admissible one-ended initial data, satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 3.1. Then (M,g)(M,g) is C2C^{2}-future-inextendible across 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}, in the sense of Definition 2.8.

Nevertheless, 𝒞​ℋΓ=∅\mathcal{CH}_{\Gamma}=\emptyset if one accepts Conjecture 1.9. Thus, this last obstruction to C2C^{2}-inextendibility should disappear with a proof of Conjecture 1.9, which would also imply the Weak Cosmic Censorship Conjecture (Conjecture 1.8). Note, however, that such a proof would require to study the space-time near the center-endpoint bΓb_{\Gamma} and thus would require different techniques than those employed in the present paper. In view of these considerations, it is interesting to use the C2C^{2}-inextendibility of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} to obtain the following “conditional” C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility of one-ended space-times:

Theorem 3.4.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be the maximal development of admissible one-ended initial data, satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 3.1 and assume moreover that 𝒞​ℋΓ=∅\mathcal{CH}_{\Gamma}=\emptyset, where 𝒞​ℋΓ\mathcal{CH}_{\Gamma} is a priori boundary component as defined in Theorem 0.1. Then (M,g)(M,g) is C2C^{2}-future-inextendible.

Remark 3.3.

In these theorems, we assumed that the asymptotic black hole charge is non-zero, which is the hardest case (and conjecturally the generic one). Recall from Remark 3.2 that if the charge is zero, then 𝒞​ℋi+=∅\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}=\emptyset. Therefore, the space-time is immediately C2C^{2}-future-inextendible in the two-ended case (and no more work is needed, see [49]). In the one-ended case, the space-time is also C2C^{2}-future-inextendible, under the same assumption as Theorem 3.4 i.e. if 𝒞​ℋΓ=∅\mathcal{CH}_{\Gamma}=\emptyset.

3.3 Classification of the Cauchy horizon emanating from i+i^{+} and estimates

In this section, we present our classification of the Cauchy horizons emanating from time-like infinity, which is fundamental to our proof of C2C^{2}-inextendibility. In what follows, we will use the generic notation 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} for any Cauchy horizon emanating from time-like infinity, be it 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} in the one-ended case (see Theorem 0.1), or 𝒞​ℋi1+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}_{1}}, 𝒞​ℋi2+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}_{2}} in the two-ended case (see Theorem 0.2). Correspondingly, ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} will be the generic notation for the corresponding event horizon, e.g. ℋ1+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{1} for 𝒞​ℋi1+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}_{1}}. In particular, we emphasize that all our subsequent results are valid both in the one-ended case, and the two-ended case. We also take the convention that the end-point of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} does not belong to 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}.

We will parametrize 1010 10 Of course, if 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is the ingoing Cauchy horizon of the one-ended case, or 𝒞​ℋi1+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}_{1}} in the two-ended case, we can chose τ=u\tau=u and ς=v\varsigma=v. 𝒞ℋi+={−∞<τ<τ𝒞​ℋi+}\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}=\{-\infty<\tau<\tau_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}\} by τ\tau and ℋ+:={ς0≤ς≤+∞}\mathcal{H}^{+}:=\{\varsigma_{0}\leq\varsigma\leq+\infty\} by ς\varsigma in this section.

We say the Cauchy horizon 𝒞ℋi+={−∞<τ<τ𝒞​ℋi+}\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}=\{-\infty<\tau<\tau_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}\} is a Cauchy Horizon of dynamical type if there exists τs∈ℝ\tau_{s}\in\mathbb{R} such that the area-radius function rr extends continuously to a function rC​H​(τ)r_{CH}(\tau) for −∞<τ≤τs-\infty<\tau\leq\tau_{s} and τ→rC​H​(τ)\tau\rightarrow r_{CH}(\tau) is strictly decreasing on (−∞,τs)(-\infty,\tau_{s}).

For the sake of simplicity and fluidity of exposition, we will assume that 12<s<1\frac{1}{2}<s<1 in the proof of the estimates of Theorem 3.5 and in fact in the rest of the paper. We can do this with no loss of generality, as this just makes the assumption in Theorem 3.1 weaker. Indeed, note that the case s≥1s\geq 1 is slightly easier and our proof works just as well in this situation.

3.4 A trapped neighborhood of the Cauchy horizon emanating from i+i^{+}

In this section, we state a side result: there exists a trapped neighborhood 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{{}^{\prime}} of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}, as depicted in Figure 4. This result, which is of independent interest, is also used as a key ingredient in the proof of the classification of Theorm 3.5.

Theorem 3.6.

We work under the assumptions of Theorem 3.1 and let 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} be either the Cauchy horizon emanating from time-like infinity in the one-ended case, or 𝒞​ℋi1+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}_{1}}, 𝒞​ℋi2+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}_{2}} in the two-ended case.
Then for every u<u𝒞​ℋi+u<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}, there exists v⁡(u)∈ℝv(u)\in\mathbb{R} such that {u}×[v(u),+∞)⊂𝒯\{u\}\times[v(u),+\infty)\subset\mathcal{T}.
In particular, there are no limit points of 𝒜\mathcal{A} on 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}.

3.5 A breakdown criterion to propagate the weak null singularity

In this last section, we present a breakdown criterion: essentially, if the Dafermos condition (1.6) is satisfied on one cone, then the Hawking mass blows up on 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}. This result is the very first step towards the proof of the existence of a trapped neighborhood, the classification of the Cauchy horizon and ultimately the inextendibility results.

Theorem 3.7.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.1, assume that one of the following (non-equivalent) conditions holds on an outgoing cone Cu0C_{u_{0}} under 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}, for some u0<u𝒞​ℋi+u_{0}<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}} (recalling the definition of κ\kappa from (2.5)):

∫v0+∞κ⁡(u0,v)​𝑑v<+∞,\int_{v_{0}}^{+\infty}\kappa(u_{0},v)dv<+\infty,
lim supv→+∞ρ⁡(u0,v)=+∞,\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}\rho(u_{0},v)=+\infty,
lim supv→+∞ϖ⁡(u0,v)=+∞,\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}\varpi(u_{0},v)=+\infty,
lim supv→+∞|ν|(u0,v)>0,\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|\nu|(u_{0},v)>0,
lim supv→+∞|ϕ|2​(u0,v)+lim supv→+∞|Q|​(u0,v)=+∞,\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|\phi|^{2}(u_{0},v)+\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|Q|(u_{0},v)=+\infty,

then for all u0≤u<u𝒞​ℋi+u_{0}\leq u<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}, both the following conditions hold

limv→+∞ρ⁡(u,v)=+∞,\lim_{v\rightarrow+\infty}\rho(u,v)=+\infty,
∫v0+∞κ⁡(u,v)​𝑑v<+∞.\int_{v_{0}}^{+\infty}\kappa(u,v)dv<+\infty.

Once this result is proven, one can establish the classification of Theorem 3.5. A posteriori, once Theorem 3.5 is also available, we obtain the following result as a corollary of Theorem 3.7:

Corollary 3.8.

We make the same assumptions as Theorem 3.7, for some u0<u𝒞​ℋi+u_{0}<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}.

Then either 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is of dynamical type, or 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is of mixed type with u0>uTu_{0}>u_{T}.

In both cases, for all u0≤u<u𝒞​ℋi+u_{0}\leq u<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}, limv→+∞|∂ur|(u,v)\lim_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|\partial_{u}r|(u,v) exists and limv→+∞|∂ur|(u,v)>0\lim_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|\partial_{u}r|(u,v)>0.

While we stated our results inductively – from the most specific (the C2C^{2} inextendibility theorems) to the most general (the breakdown criterion) – we will, understandably, prove them deductively, starting from Theorem 3.7 and finishing with Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 3.4. We refer to section 1.6 for the logic of the proof.

Lemma 5.5 concludes the proof of Theorem 5.4 in the case u0≤usu_{0}\leq u_{s}. The harder case u0>usu_{0}>u_{s} remains. We will address it in the next two lemma, using Lemma 5.5 as a building block.

The objective is to use bootstrap method, which we write in detail. We introduce a set ℬv0\mathcal{B}_{v_{0}} over which certain estimates are satisfied. We prove that

  1. 1.

    The set {(u,∞),u∈ℬv0}⊂𝒞​ℋi+\{(u,\infty),u\in\mathcal{B}_{v_{0}}\}\subset\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is “static” i.e. all quantities coincide with their Reissner–Nordström counterparts, like in statement 2 from Lemma 5.5. Moreover, estimates analogous to those of Lemma 5.5 are true ℬv0\mathcal{B}_{v_{0}}.

  2. 2.

    ℬv0\mathcal{B}_{v_{0}} is entirely included in the trapped region, using the lower bound (5.1) of section 5.1.

  3. 3.

    There exists a strictly bigger open set ℬv0′⊃ℬv0\mathcal{B}^{\prime}_{v_{0}}\supset\mathcal{B}_{v_{0}}, which is trapped, hence has finite volume.

  4. 4.

    L1L^{1}-type estimates are true on ℬv0′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}_{v_{0}} and they imply (5.30) and (5.31) on ℬv0′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}_{v_{0}}.

    As a consequence of these four facts, we will show that ℬv0\mathcal{B}_{v_{0}} is both open and closed, concluding the bootstrap-type argument; therefore ℬv0=[us,u0]\mathcal{B}_{v_{0}}=[u_{s},u_{0}], which concludes the proof of Theorem 5.4.

The proof of step 1, together with the definition of the set ℬv0\mathcal{B}_{v_{0}}, is the object of the following lemma:

and ℬv0\mathcal{B}_{v_{0}}, the set of u∈[us,u0]u\in[u_{s},u_{0}] such that the estimates (5.30), (5.31) hold on the rectangle [us,u]×[v0,+∞)[u_{s},u]\times[v_{0},+\infty).

In the last part of the proof of Theorem 5.4, we prove step 4 and conclude the bootstrap argument. The L1L^{1}-type estimates, using finiteness of the space-time volume of [us,u+ϵ0]×[v0,+∞][u_{s},u+\epsilon_{0}]\times[v_{0},+\infty] proven in step 3, are inspired by the work 1515 15 Precisely Lemma 10.3, in which it is assumed that the rectangle has finite volume. The finiteness of the volume is later obtained by a different argument, using a monotonicity property specific to the uncharged and massless considered in [32]. of Luk and Oh [32] on uncharged and massless scalar fields.

Some important modifications are, however, carried out to accommodate the case of a variable charge . First, we also couple the L1L^{1} estimates with bootstraped L∞L^{\infty} estimates on QQ (because the field is charged) and L∞L^{\infty} estimates on ϕ\phi (because the field is massive). In view of the slow decay assumed on the event horizon, consistent with the expected decay of massive and/or charged fields c.f. section 1.5.1, the analogue of estimates (10.6) and (10.7) of Lemma 10.3 of [32] do not hold, because ∂vlog⁡(Ω2)−2​K−\partial_{v}\log(\Omega^{2})-2K- and ∂vϕ\partial_{v}\phi are no longer integrable in the case s<1s<1 (this is expected for massive and charged scalar fields). 5.3 Static points and Dafermos points

Recall that the “staticity condition” (5.2), which is equivalent to (1.21) (see section 2), is gauge-independent (see the discussion in section 1.6). It was first introduced by Dafermos in [13], in the context of his proof of mass inflation in the interior of dynamical black holes, for the Einstein–Maxwell-(uncharged)-scalar-field model. While Dafermos does not use of this staticity condition (5.2) in his proof, he effectively produces 1616 16 Making point-wise lower bounds assumptions on the scalar field on the event horizon, and exploiting a special monotonicity property which is specific to the uncharged and massless case. a connected portion of the Cauchy horizon on which condition (5.2) is violated, for all u0≤usu_{0}\leq u_{s}, for some us∈ℝu_{s}\in\mathbb{R}. Dafermos notices the difference between the space-time he constructs, for which (5.2) is never 1717 17 As noticed in [16], the monotonicity of the Hawking mass in the uncharged and massless case allows to propagate the mass blow-up to the entire Cauchy horizon, which implies that condition (5.2) is violated everywhere on 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} for the space-times under consideration. This technique does not, however, survive when the field is massive and/or charged. satisfied, and the Reissner–Nordström space-time, which satisfies condition (5.2) for all u0∈ℝu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}. We now introduce the set of “static points on 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}” for which (5.2) is true:

Definition 5.1.

For u0∈ℝu_{0}\in\mathbb{R} and (u0,v=+∞)∈𝒞​ℋi+(u_{0},v=+\infty)\in\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}, we say that (u0,+∞)(u_{0},+\infty) is a static point of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} if the condition (5.2) is true at u0u_{0}, for some v∈ℝv\in\mathbb{R}. We define the static set 𝒮0⊂𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{S}_{0}\subset\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} as the collection of static points of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}. By abuse of notation, we also denote 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}, the projection of 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} on its first component: {u0,(u0,+∞)∈𝒮0}\{u_{0},\hskip 2.84526pt(u_{0},+\infty)\in\mathcal{S}_{0}\}.

7 Propagation of the mass blow-up, proof of Theorems 3.6 and 3.7

Once we know that the Hawking mass blows up (locally) for Cauchy horizon of dynamical or mixed type (section 6), we have to prove that this blow up is propagated (section 7.1). We will then use this result to prove Theorems 3.6 (section 7.2) and Theorem 3.7 (section 7.3).

We start by Lemma 7.1, our result proving the propagation of the blow up on the Hawking mass ρ\rho on 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}. This statement is quite general: we do not, in fact, require the assumption of Theorem 3.1 to obtain its conclusions, nor the formalism of the classification of the Cauchy horizon of Corollary 5.10. 7.2 Proof of Theorem 3.7

In this section, we return to the main proof and we work again under the assumptions of Corollary 5.10 (i.e. the assumptions of Theorem 3.1). We will use Lemma 5.6 and Corollary 5.10 to obtain a proof a Theorem 3.7 in the following proposition:

Proposition 7.2.

Assume that one of the following conditions holds for some u0<u𝒞​ℋi+u_{0}<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}:

lim supv→+∞ρ⁡(u0,v)=+∞,\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}\rho(u_{0},v)=+\infty, (7.6)
lim supv→+∞ϖ⁡(u0,v)=+∞,\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}\varpi(u_{0},v)=+\infty, (7.7)
∫v0+∞κ⁡(u0,v)<+∞,\int_{v_{0}}^{+\infty}\kappa(u_{0},v)<+\infty, (7.8)
lim supv→+∞|ν|(u0,v)>0,\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|\nu|(u_{0},v)>0, (7.9)
lim supv→+∞|ϕ|2​(u0,v)+lim supv→+∞|Q|​(u0,v)=+∞.\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|\phi|^{2}(u_{0},v)+\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}|Q|(u_{0},v)=+\infty. (7.10)

Then 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is either of dynamical type, or of mixed type, with uT<u0u_{T}<u_{0}. In any case, we have for all u≥u0u\geq u_{0} :

limv→+∞ρ⁡(u,v)=+∞,\lim_{v\rightarrow+\infty}\rho(u,v)=+\infty, (7.11)
limv→+∞ϖ⁡(u,v)=+∞,\lim_{v\rightarrow+\infty}\varpi(u,v)=+\infty, (7.12)
∫v+∞κ⁡(u,v′)​d​v′<+∞.\int_{v}^{+\infty}\kappa(u,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}<+\infty. (7.13)
Proof.

Clearly, if 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} was of static type, then by Corollary 5.10, none of condition (7.6), (7.7), (7.8), (7.9), (7.10) are possible. If 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is of mixed type, then again by Corollary 5.10, it means that u0>uTu_{0}>u_{T}, otherwise none of condition (7.6), (7.7), (7.8), (7.9), (7.10) are possible. Thus, [u0,u𝒞​ℋi+]⊂𝒞​ℋi+−𝒮0[u_{0},u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}]\subset\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}-\mathcal{S}_{0} hence (7.13) is satisfied for all u≥u0u\geq u_{0}.

To prove (7.11), we start by the case that 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is of dynamical type: then, using Lemma 6.1, we see that we have the blow up limv→+∞ρ⁡(us,v)=+∞\lim_{v\rightarrow+\infty}\rho(u_{s},v)=+\infty and by (4.8), (7.1) is satisfied: thus we can apply Lemma 7.1 thus (7.11) and a forciori (7.12) follow. If now 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is of mixed type: then, using Lemma 6.2, then we obtain the same result.

∎

7.3 Proof of Theorem 3.6

Now, as a second consequence of Lemma 5.6, we obtain the existence of a trapped neighbohood of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}:

Proposition 7.3.

For all u<u𝒞​ℋi+u<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}, there exists v⁡(u)∈ℝv(u)\in\mathbb{R} such that {u}×[v(u),+∞)⊂𝒯\{u\}\times[v(u),+\infty)\subset\mathcal{T}.

Proof.

From the estimates of [47], we know that {(u,v),v≥vγ(u),−∞<u≤us}⊂𝒯\{(u,v),v\geq v_{\gamma}(u),-\infty<u\leq u_{s}\}\subset\mathcal{T}. Now there are three cases:

  1. a

    𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is of static type.

    Then 𝒮=(−∞,u𝒞​ℋi+)\mathcal{S}=(-\infty,u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}) and the claim is given statement 1 by Theorem 5.4.

  2. b

    𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is of dynamical type.

    Then 𝒮=∅\mathcal{S}=\emptyset. By Lemma 6.1, for all u≤usu\leq u_{s}, v≥vγ​(u)v\geq v_{\gamma}(u), (6.1) is true. Thus, also using (4.8), the assumptions of Lemma 7.1 are satisfied for u1=usu_{1}=u_{s}. Recall that (u,v)∈𝒯(u,v)\in\mathcal{T} if and only if 2​ρ​(u,v)>r⁡(u,v)2\rho(u,v)>r(u,v). Since rr is bounded, then for all u<u𝒞​ℋi+u<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}, there exists v⁡(u)v(u) such that [us,u]×[v(u),+∞)⊂𝒯[u_{s},u]\times[v(u),+\infty)\subset\mathcal{T}.

  3. c

    𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} is of mixed type.

    Then 𝒮=(−∞,uT]\mathcal{S}=(-\infty,u_{T}] and by Lemma (6.2) there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that (6.5) is true at u=uT+ϵu=u_{T}+\epsilon, together with (5.16). Thus, the assumptions of Lemma 7.1 are satisfied for u1=uT+ϵu_{1}=u_{T}+\epsilon, which gives the result, as in case b.

∎

8 Quantitative estimates and proof of Theorem 3.5

Now we establish quantitative estimates on an arbitrarily late portion of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}. The key ingredient in our proof is the presence of a trapped neighborhood of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} obtained in Theorem 3.6, whose volume is thus finite. While such estimates are not strictly speaking necessary to prove C2C^{2}-inextendibility (but we choose to prove inextendibility using them), they bridge the gap between the (preliminary) classification of Theorem 5.4 and the final classification of Theorem 3.5.

8.1 L1L^{1} and L∞L^{\infty} estimates for a trapped rectangle

In this section, we prove L1L^{1} estimates on a trapped 1919 19 In particular RR is of finite space-time volume, but as we shall see, the stronger assumption R⊂𝒯R\subset\mathcal{T} turns out to be necessary to our method. rectangle RR which includes a portion of 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}. These estimates are in the vein of those of Lemma 5.8 but we introduce a considerable difficulty, to accommodate the case of a Cauchy horizon of dynamical type 2020 20 Recall that, in retrospect, Lemma 5.8 was concerned by Cauchy horizon of mixed type: in this case, ϕ\phi and QQ were necessarily bounded.: both ϕ\phi and QQ are allowed to blow up, at a polynomial rate. While this seems anecdotal, we cannot close the estimates of Lemma 5.8 because we start with weaker assumptions (8.5), (8.6) and we must get contend 2121 21 The lack of integrability when s<1s<1, even if ϕ\phi is bounded, was a new difficulty in Lemma 5.8 already, compared to Lemma 10.3 of [32]. with even weaker estimates. Allowing for this possibility is not necessary to prove Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 3.3, as we already know that the mass blows up by Lemma 7.1 but is crucial 2222 22 This is because we require estimates, even weak ones, just to prove that ν\nu has a non-zero limit on 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}. to proving Theorem 3.5.

for some C=C⁡(M,e,q0,m2,u1,um​a​x,v1,D)>0C=C(M,e,q_{0},m^{2},u_{1},u_{max},v_{1},D)>0. This estimate plays a crucial role in the inextendibility argument of [26].

Remark 8.2.

A slight modification of the argument allows to prove Lemma 8.1 in the case 12<s≤34\frac{1}{2}<s\leq\frac{3}{4}. We shall not pursue this route, for simplicity and because in practice we expect s>34s>\frac{3}{4} in any cases of physical interest.

8.2 Concluding the proof of Theorem 3.5

Now, we are ready to establish the quantitative estimates of Theorem 3.5:

Proposition 8.2.

For all u1<u2<u𝒞​ℋi+u_{1}<u_{2}<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}, there exists C⁡(M,e,q0,m2,u1,u2,s)>0C(M,e,q_{0},m^{2},u_{1},u_{2},s)>0 such that for all u1≤u≤u2u_{1}\leq u\leq u_{2} and v≥v⁡(u)v\geq v(u), the estimates (3.8), (3.9), (3.10), (3.11), (3.12), (3.13), (3.14), (3.15), (3.16), (3.17), (3.18) hold.

9 Global inextendibility across the Cauchy horizon and proof of
Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 3.4

In this section, we present a geometric proof of C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility under various assumptions. We only require very soft geometric arguments, as the quantitative estimates were already obtained in section 8. While these quantitative estimates are very different from their uncharged counterparts, in the absence of certain simplifying mechanisms such as monotonicity, the geometric argument is extremely similar to what was used in [32] to prove C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility in the uncharged case. In this section, we rely on the blow up of the Ricci curvature given by (3.18) to obtain C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility and for this purpose, we adapt marginally the argument of Luk and Oh from [32] to our setting.

9.1 C2C^{2}-inextendibility in the two-ended case

We start with the two-ended case. First, we need a result from [32]:

Proposition 9.1 ([32], section 11).

We consider (M,gμ​ν,ϕ,F)(M,g_{\mu\nu},\phi,F) the maximal development of smooth, spherically symmetric and admissible two-ended initial data. Assume that (M,g)(M,g) is C2C^{2}-future-extendible in the sense of Definition 2.7.

Then 2424 24 Strictly speaking, the result in [32] is Lemma 11.5, which presents an alternative between two possibilities, one of them of the statement of Proposition 9.1, and the other one is proven to be impossible in Lemma 11.6, using soft estimates present in [28]., there exists p∈𝒞​ℋi1+∪𝒞​ℋi2+p\in\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}_{1}}\cup\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}_{2}} and a future-directed null geodesic γ:(−ϵ,ϵ)→M~\gamma:(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\rightarrow\tilde{M} such that

  1. 1.

    γ⁡(−ϵ,0)⊂M\gamma(-\epsilon,0)\subset M.

  2. 2.

    γ|(−ϵ,0)\gamma_{|(-\epsilon,0)} is radial.

  3. 3.

    Π∘γ|(−ϵ,0)⊂{(up,v),v≥v0}\Pi\circ\gamma_{|(-\epsilon,0)}\subset\{(u_{p},v),v\geq v_{0}\} for up<u𝒞​ℋi+u_{p}<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}, such that p=(up,+∞)p=(u_{p},+\infty) in (u,v)(u,v) coordinates and v0∈ℝv_{0}\in\mathbb{R}.

  4. 4.

    For all −ϵ<t<0-\epsilon<t<0, we have dd​t(Π∘γ(t))=c⋅Ω−2(Π∘γ(t))∂v\frac{d}{dt}(\Pi\circ\gamma(t))=c\cdot\Omega^{-2}(\Pi\circ\gamma(t))\partial_{v} for some c>0c>0.

  5. 5.

    t→R​i​c​(γ˙​(t),γ˙​(t))=c2⋅Ω−4​|∂vϕ|2t\rightarrow Ric(\dot{\gamma}(t),\dot{\gamma}(t))=c^{2}\cdot\Omega^{-4}|\partial_{v}\phi|^{2} is bounded on (−ϵ,0)(-\epsilon,0).

While Proposition 9.1 is proved in the context of an uncharged and massless scalar fields in [32], it does not rely on the precise matter model, and only assumes spherical symmetry and the a priori boundary characterization in the two-ended case of Theorem 0.2, which is also valid for the charged and/or massive scalar field model, c.f. [28]. Therefore, Proposition 9.1 holds in our context, with the same proof.

Proposition 9.2.

Under the same assumptions as Proposition 9.1, we have the following blow up of the Ricci curvature:

lim supv→+∞Ric(Ω−2∂v,Ω−2∂v)(up,v)=+∞.\limsup_{v\rightarrow+\infty}Ric(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v},\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v})(u_{p},v)=+\infty.

This contradicts statement 5 of Proposition 9.1, thus by contradiction (M,g)(M,g) is C2C^{2}-future-inextendible.

Proof.

The proof follows immediately from (3.18): by the pigeon-hole principle, there exists a dyadic sequence vn=2n⋅v⁡(u)v_{n}=2^{n}\cdot v(u) such that R​i​c​(V,V)​(u,vn)≥C⋅vn−1⋅e1.98​|K−|⋅vnRic(V,V)(u,v_{n})\geq C\cdot v_{n}^{-1}\cdot e^{1.98|K_{-}|\cdot v_{n}} for all u<u𝒞​ℋi+u<u_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}; so in particular at (up,+∞)∈𝒞​ℋi+(u_{p},+\infty)\in\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}, hence the lim sup\limsup is infinite, as claimed, and the contradiction follows.

∎

Proposition 9.2 provides a proof of Theorem 3.2.

9.2 C2C^{2}-inextendibility across the Cauchy horizon in the one-ended case

As we have seen, the two-ended case follows immediately from (3.18), as we used directly the geometric setting of [32]. In the one-ended case, we have to re-prove some of the claims of [32], but the approach is essentially similar and, as before, the key ingredient is the blow up of the Ricci curvature given by (3.18). Before going to the proof, we recall a Lemma from Dafermos–Rendall [18] concerning C2C^{2} extensions, which appears also as Lemma 11.2 in [32]:

Lemma 9.3 ([18], Lemma 11.2 in [32]).

If M~\tilde{M} is a C2C^{2} extension, the standard rotations extend continuously to ∂M\partial M. ∂M\partial M is the boundary of MM inside a C2C^{2} extension M~\tilde{M}.

As a result, we obtain immediately the following corollary on the projection on the quotiented space-time:

9.3 C2C^{2}-inextendibility if 𝒞​ℋΓ=∅\mathcal{CH}_{\Gamma}=\emptyset in the one-ended case

Now, we turn to the C2C^{2}-future-inextendibility of the space-time in the one-ended case, if we assume additionally that the “Cauchy horizon emanating from the center” 𝒞​ℋΓ\mathcal{CH}_{\Gamma} is empty, an assumption which is conjectured to be generic (see Conjecture 1.9, and related to Weak Cosmic Censorship, see section 1.5. The proof is similar to that of section 9.2.

Proposition 9.7.

We consider (M,gμ​ν,ϕ,F)(M,g_{\mu\nu},\phi,F) the maximal development of smooth, spherically symmetric and admissible one-ended initial data with a priori boundary ℬ+\mathcal{B^{+}} given by the decomposition of Theorem 0.1.

Proof.

Since ∂M\partial M is Liptschitz (Lemma 11.1 in [32]), by the Rademacher theorem it is almost everywhere differentiable, so one can find p∈∂Mp\in\partial M at which ∂M\partial M is differentiable (c.f. [32]). Since rr extends continuously to ∂M\partial M (Lemma 11.3 in [32]), we either have r⁡(p)≠0r(p)\neq 0 or r⁡(p)=0r(p)=0. If r⁡(p)≠0r(p)\neq 0, then by Theorem 0.1, p∈𝒞​ℋi+p\in\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}} since 𝒞​ℋΓ=∅\mathcal{CH}_{\Gamma}=\emptyset. In this case, one obtains a contradiction using the same argument as in Proposition 9.5 and Proposition 9.6. So we can assume for now that r⁡(p)=0r(p)=0. Then, we can repeat the argument of Lemma 11.5 of [32], which yields the result. ∎

To obtain the result, one can use a Lemma from [32], proven in the very same way:

Lemma 9.8 (Lemma 11.6, [32]).

The existence of a time-like geodesic γ:(−ϵ,ϵ)→M~\gamma:(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\rightarrow\tilde{M} such that γ⁡(0)=p\gamma(0)=p, r⁡(p)=0r(p)=0 and γ⁡((,,,))⊂M\gamma((-\epsilon,0))\subset M contradicts the fact that M~\tilde{M} is a C2C^{2} extension.

As for Proposition 9.1, this result does not use the specific structure of the uncharged massless field equations and is also valid in our context, as it only uses soft estimates (namely the blow-up of the Kretschmann scalar at boundary points pp where r⁡(p)=0r(p)=0) which were already proven in [28]. Proposition 9.7 and Lemma 9.8 provide a proof of Theorem 3.4.

Appendix A Construction of a Cauchy horizon of mixed type for the Einstein-null-dust model

In this appendix, we construct an example of a Cauchy horizon of mixed type, following Definition 3.3. In the second part of our development, we prove the blow up of the Hawking mass for mixed and dynamical type Cauchy horizons in the Einstein–Maxwell-null-dust model, following Poisson and Israel [43] and 2626 26 Note that Ori considers Cauchy horizons of mixed type in [37]. Ori [37], the first instances of the mass inflation scenario in the literature. Notice that their model is very elementary, as the dust clouds are simply transported linearly in the null directions, and only interact indirectly, via the metric: thus, the “scattering theory” is trivial. Additionally, such a model does not allow for one-ended regular solutions, unlike the charged/massive scalar field model. In this appendix we sketch a mathematical proof of mass inflation, using the methods of [47]; this is also an opportunity to illustrate the terminology of the present paper in the simpler setting of dust, where little analysis is required and monotonicity suffices. κ−1​(U,v)≳e|K−|​(M,e)​v⋅∫Uγ⁡(v)UφR2​(U′)​d​U′=e|K−|​(M,e)​v⋅∫Uγ⁡(v)Ur2​(U′,v0)⋅(fR0​(U′))2​d​U′≳e|K−|​(M,e)​v⋅∫Uγ⁡(v)U(fR0​(U′))2​d​U′.\kappa^{-1}(U,v)\gtrsim e^{|K_{-}|(M,e)v}\cdot\int_{U_{\gamma(v)}}^{U}\varphi_{R}^{2}(U^{\prime})dU^{\prime}=e^{|K_{-}|(M,e)v}\cdot\int_{U_{\gamma(v)}}^{U}r^{2}(U^{\prime},v_{0})\cdot(f_{R}^{0}(U^{\prime}))^{2}dU^{\prime}\gtrsim e^{|K_{-}|(M,e)v}\cdot\int_{U_{\gamma(v)}}^{U}(f_{R}^{0}(U^{\prime}))^{2}dU^{\prime}. (A.13)

Then, there are our three possibilities, starting with the easiest:

  1. 1.

    Dynamical case: then for all U∈[0,Um​a​x)U\in[0,U_{max}), ∫0U(fR0)2​(U′)​d​U′>0\int_{0}^{U}(f^{0}_{R})^{2}(U^{\prime})dU^{\prime}>0.

    Indeed by (a), for all U∈[0,Um​a​x)U\in[0,U_{max}), there exists U′<UU^{\prime}<U with (fR0​(U′))2>0(f^{0}_{R}(U^{\prime}))^{2}>0, hence by continuity there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that (fR0​(U′))2>0(f^{0}_{R}(U^{\prime}))^{2}>0 on [U′,U′+ϵ][U^{\prime},U^{\prime}+\epsilon], which implies ∫0U(fR0)2​(U′)​d​U′>0\int_{0}^{U}(f^{0}_{R})^{2}(U^{\prime})dU^{\prime}>0 .

    In view of the limit Uγ​(v)→0U_{\gamma}(v)\rightarrow 0 as v→+∞v\rightarrow+\infty (recall that γ\gamma terminates at i+i^{+}) then limv→+∞∫Uγ⁡(v)U(fR0​(U′))2​d​U′>0\lim_{v\rightarrow+\infty}\int_{U_{\gamma(v)}}^{U}(f_{R}^{0}(U^{\prime}))^{2}dU^{\prime}>0 for all U∈[0,Um​a​x)U\in[0,U_{max}), hence κ−1​(U,v)→+∞\kappa^{-1}(U,v)\rightarrow+\infty. If νC​H​(U)=0\nu_{CH}(U)=0 for some 0<U<Um​a​x0<U<U_{max}, then (A.12) is contradicted (after dividing both sides of (A.12) by r​Ω2r\Omega^{2}). Hence ν𝒞​ℋi+​(U)<0\nu_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}(U)<0 for all U∈[0,Um​a​x]U\in[0,U_{max}] thus r𝒞​ℋi+r_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}} is strictly decreasing on [0,Um​a​x)[0,U_{max}) as desired . Moreover κ−1​(U,v)∼4​|νl|​(U)Ω2​(U,v)\kappa^{-1}(U,v)\sim\frac{4|\nu_{l}|(U)}{\Omega^{2}(U,v)} by (A.12).

    If additionally we have a lower bound fL0​(v)=C⋅v−s+o⁡(v−s)f_{L}^{0}(v)=C\cdot v^{-s}+o(v^{-s}) then by the stability estimates of [47], −λ∼C⋅v−2​s-\lambda\sim C\cdot v^{-2s}, at least for UU small enough and in the future of the curve γ\gamma. Since 2​ρ−r=κ−1⋅(−λ)2\rho-r=\kappa^{-1}\cdot(-\lambda), ρ⁡(U,v)→+∞\rho(U,v)\rightarrow+\infty as v→+∞v\rightarrow+\infty, for small UU. A forciciori, ϖ⁡(U,v)→+∞\varpi(U,v)\rightarrow+\infty for small UU, and by the monotonicity of (A.3), ϖ⁡(U,v)→+∞\varpi(U,v)\rightarrow+\infty for all U∈[0,Um​a​x)U\in[0,U_{max}). Hence, for all U∈[0,Um​a​x)U\in[0,U_{max}), ρ⁡(U,v)→+∞\rho(U,v)\rightarrow+\infty as v→+∞v\rightarrow+\infty.

  2. 2.

    Static case: for all U∈[0,Um​a​x)U\in[0,U_{max}), fR0​(U)=0f^{0}_{R}(U)=0.

    Then κ⁡(U,v)=1\kappa(U,v)=1 as ∂U(κ−1)=0\partial_{U}(\kappa^{-1})=0. By (A.12), it means that ν𝒞​ℋi+​(U)=0\nu_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}(U)=0 for all U∈[0,Um​a​x)U\in[0,U_{max}) hence r𝒞​ℋi+r_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}} is constant and by (A.3) ϖ𝒞​ℋi+\varpi_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}} is constant. Their values are r𝒞​ℋi+≡r−​(M,e)>0r_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}\equiv r_{-}(M,e)>0 and ϖ𝒞​ℋi+≡M>0\varpi_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}\equiv M>0 by the stability estimates of [47]. This implies that ρ\rho is constant on 𝒞​ℋi+\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}: ρ⁡(U,v)→M−e2r−​(M,e)\rho(U,v)\rightarrow M-\frac{e^{2}}{r_{-}(M,e)} as v→+∞v\rightarrow+\infty for all U∈[0,Um​a​x)U\in[0,U_{max}).

  3. 3.

    Mixed case: ∫0UT(fR0)2​(U′)​d​U′=0\int_{0}^{U_{T}}(f^{0}_{R})^{2}(U^{\prime})dU^{\prime}=0 but ∫UTU(fR0)2​(U′)​d​U′>0\int_{U_{T}}^{U}(f^{0}_{R})^{2}(U^{\prime})dU^{\prime}>0 for all UT<U<Um​a​xU_{T}<U<U_{max}.

    Indeed, the above statement follows from the same logic as for the dynamical case, see earlier discussion.

    Then similarly, r𝒞​ℋi+​(U)=r−​(M,e)r_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}(U)=r_{-}(M,e), ϖ𝒞​ℋi+​(U)=M\varpi_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}(U)=M, and ρ𝒞​ℋi+​(U)=M−e2r−​(M,e)\rho_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}(U)=M-\frac{e^{2}}{r_{-}(M,e)} for all U∈[0,UT]U\in[0,U_{T}]. Yet, κ−1​(U,v)→+∞\kappa^{-1}(U,v)\rightarrow+\infty for all U∈(UT,Um​a​x)U\in(U_{T},U_{max}), as ∫0U(fR0​(U′))2​d​U′>0\int_{0}^{U}(f_{R}^{0}(U^{\prime}))^{2}dU^{\prime}>0. Thus ν𝒞​ℋi+​(U)<0\nu_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}}(U)<0 for all U∈(UT,Um​a​x)U\in(U_{T},U_{max}) and r𝒞​ℋi+r_{\mathcal{CH}_{i^{+}}} is strictly decreasing on (UT,Um​a​x)(U_{T},U_{max}). If additionally we have a lower bound fL0​(v)=C⋅v−s+o⁡(v−s)f_{L}^{0}(v)=C\cdot v^{-s}+o(v^{-s}), then we have the blow up of ρ\rho, as in the dynamical case.

∎

Remark A.2.

Notice that the proof was considerably easier for the uncharged dust than for a charged scalar field, as we used in this section some special monotonicity properties that are not exploitable in the charged case. In contrast, in the earlier sections, we proved estimates that were harder to obtain but also more robust as they do not rely on monotonicity.
